question: Would a life that never ended eventually become unbearable?
answer: Bernard Williams took Elina Makropulos, held at 42 by an elixir for three centuries, who refuses more: everything has happened to her before. A self that keeps its character runs out of new desires; a self that keeps changing is not really you surviving. Either way, endless life loses what made you want it.
move: It turns on whether the best goods wear out with repetition.
counterpoint: Boredom is a fact about some pleasures, not about life. Many goods renew themselves: a favourite piece of music, a meal with friends, a walk by the sea are wanted again and again, as John Martin Fischer argued in 1994. An endless life could be a rhythm of such returns, not a queue of used-up novelties.
reference: Williams, The Makropulos Case: Reflections on the Tedium of Immortality, in Problems of the Self, Cambridge University Press, 1973; Fischer, Why Immortality Is Not So Bad, International Journal of Philosophical Studies 2, 1994
